To fix (3)

To fix Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

Show details

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

All participants provided informed consent and received financial compensation.

Primary English-speaking U.S. residents were recruited, targeting at least 30 participants per stimulus (Hehman et al., 2018; Stolier et al., 2018) and oversampling to account for exclusions.

A total of 150 participants were recruited via Prolific (Mage = 41.31, SDage = 14.50; two implausible age responses excluded; 93 females, 56 males, 1 another gender; 113 White, 17 Black, 5 Asian, 10 Multiracial, 5 another race).

Participants were randomly assigned to evaluate a subset of 360 stimuli comprising 20 male and 20 female images in each of the three cropping conditions (full-face, face-without-eyes, eyes-only).

Before beginning, participants were informed that they would view images of faces or eyes displaying different mental state expressions and were instructed to identify the depicted mental state (“What is this person’s mental state experience?”).

Follow-up pairwise comparisons with Holm correction showed that participants were significantly more accurate in identifying mental states when viewing full faces than when viewing eyes-only, t(149) = 14.19, p < .001, or faces-without-eyes, t(149) = 8.27, p < .001.

A total of 451 participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk.

Each participant completed a face similarity judgment task followed by a conceptual association task.

We recruited 221 participants from Prolific.

Participants completed 10 practice trials, each randomly drawing from the 15 mental states in their assigned subset.

Thus, participants completed 30 face-judgment trials.

Following the face judgments task, participants completed a conceptual association task similar to the one used in Study 2.

Trial order and the left-right ordering of the two states within each trial were randomized.

Mental state pairs believed to be more likely to co-occur were more frequently confused in face judgments, and participants were more likely to select a particular incorrect state when they viewed it as more strongly associated with the depicted state, even after accounting for shared associations.

Because the study included two versions with different stimuli, we recruited a total of 102 participants through Prolific.

Because this set was too large for a single session, we randomly divided the stimuli into two subsets of 75 faces (five per state), and participants were assigned to one version.

When two states were more conceptually related, participants were more likely to confuse those states when judging naturalistic facial expressions.

Thus, even for naturalistic, unposed faces, participants were more likely to make a particular confusion when they personally viewed the depicted and selected states as more strongly associated than other participants did.

In Study 1, participants were more accurate in identifying mental states from full faces than from partial faces or isolated eye regions.

Studies 3 and 4 extended this relationship to specific mental state confusions: participants were more likely to misidentify a depicted state as another state when the two were more strongly conceptually associated.

To check (4)

To check Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests

What we found

We found 3 t-tests and/or F-tests where effect sizes are not reported. Check these tests in the table below, and consider adding effect sizes.

Show details

We recommend checking the sentences below, and add any missing effect sizes.

For t-tests with a reported d, coherence checks yielded 3 matches under assumptions, 2 indeterminate cases.
Follow-up pairwise comparisons with Holm correction showed that participants were significantly more accurate in identifying mental states when viewing full faces than when viewing eyes-only, t(149) = 14.19, p < .001, or faces-without-eyes, t(149) = 8.27, p < .001.
Follow-up pairwise comparisons with Holm correction showed that participants were significantly more accurate in identifying mental states when viewing full faces than when viewing eyes-only, t(149) = 14.19, p < .001, or faces-without-eyes, t(149) = 8.27, p < .001.
Perhaps surprisingly, accuracy in the facewithout-eyes condition was also significantly higher than in the eyes-only condition, t(149) = 6.26, p < .001, highlighting the importance of cues beyond the eye region in facilitating mental state inferences.

For metascientific articles demonstrating that effect sizes are often not reported:

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 2 code files.

File name setwd() calls found
Study4_analysis.R setwd(here::here(“S4”, “data”))
Study3_analysis.R setwd(here::here(“S3”, “data”))

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 3 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

Reproducible Environment

Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 25 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script downloads data while it runs.

  • Study1_analysis.R

Online files can move, change or disappear. Save the downloaded files, add them to the deposit, and let the script read the saved copies.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

  • Figure_combined_S3_S4.R

The error message of each script is in the table above.

Other problems in the files

  • Study3_analysis.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.
  • Study4_analysis.R calls setwd(), which ties the script to a folder on the author’s computer. We replaced the call with one that does nothing so the script could run; it should be removed from the script.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 5 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 Study1_analysis.R — numeric
2 Study2_analysis.R — numeric
3 Study3_analysis.R — numeric
4 Study4_analysis.R — numeric
5 Figure_combined_S3_S4.R Study3_analysis.R, Study4_analysis.R dependency

File paths

18 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: data_attn_v1.csv to S4/data/data_attn_v1.csv (in Study4_analysis.R); data_attn_v2.csv to S4/data/data_attn_v2.csv (in Study4_analysis.R); conceptual_long_v1.csv to S4/data/conceptual_long_v1.csv (in Study4_analysis.R); conceptual_long_v2.csv to S4/data/conceptual_long_v2.csv (in Study4_analysis.R); perceptual_long_v1.csv to S4/data/perceptual_long_v1.csv (in Study4_analysis.R); perceptual_long_v2.csv to S4/data/perceptual_long_v2.csv (in Study4_analysis.R); demos1.csv to S3/data/demos1.csv (in Study3_analysis.R); demos2.csv to S3/data/demos2.csv (in Study3_analysis.R); demos3.csv to S3/data/demos3.csv (in Study3_analysis.R); demos4.csv to S3/data/demos4.csv (in Study3_analysis.R), and 8 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 5 scripts: 3 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. 1 script needs the internet, which is off during the run: Study1_analysis.R. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this.

File Outcome Detail Time (s)
Study1_analysis.R needs_internet 7.3
Study2_analysis.R ran_ok 14.4
Study3_analysis.R ran_ok 22.4
Study4_analysis.R ran_ok 15.5
Figure_combined_S3_S4.R errored runtime 2.9

setwd() in the code

2 scripts call setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Reproducible after removing setwd(): Study4_analysis.R, Study3_analysis.R.

File setwd() removed Path(s) it set

>     t_out  <- t.test(vals, mu = 0.25, alternative = "greater")
>     
>     results <- results %>%
>       bind_rows(data.frame(
>         subID   = id,
>         mean    = mean(vals),
>         SD      = sd(vals),
>         N       = length(vals),
>         p_value = t_out$p.value,
>         stringsAsFactors = FALSE
>       ))
>   }
>   
>   # Rename columns with condition suffix for clarity when merging
>   names(results)[2:5] <- paste0(names(results)[2:5], "_", suffix)
>   return(results)
> }

More detail

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
