How Ethics Approval Check works

This module searches for statements of ethics approval, IRB approval, institutional review board approval, and related terms.

Patterns are designed to capture:

Human research committee names - Institutional Review Board / IRB (US standard) - Independent Ethics Committee / IEC (ICH-GCP international clinical trial term) - Ethical/Ethics Review Board (generic) - Ethics (Advisory/Review) Committee/Board/Panel/Sub-committee - Research Ethics Committee/Board/Panel (UK/Canada/Australia) - Medical Ethics Committee - Human Subjects/Research Committee / Human Research Ethics (Advisory) Panel - Committee for/on the Protection of Human Subjects - Committee on (Health) Research Ethics - Office of Research Ethics - Abbreviations: IEC, REC, REB, ERB, METC, DEC. REC/REB/ERB/DEC are short enough to collide with unrelated jargon (e.g. REC as a recognition-heuristic model abbreviation, DEC as a decision-task label, Reb as an author surname), so these four require an ethics/approval/committee/board/panel/institutional/ protocol word within ~30 characters in the same sentence. IRB and IEC are kept unconstrained as they are not observed to collide in practice. - Dutch: Medisch-ethische toetsingscommissie (METC) - French: Comité d'éthique / Comité d'Ethique

Animal research committee names - Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee / IACUC (US standard) - Any sentence containing animal(s) and committee (or board/panel) within ~5 words of each other — catches Experimental Animal Care and Use Committee, Animal Ethics Committee, Animal Welfare Board, Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body, etc. - UK: Animal Welfare Ethical Review Body / AWERB - Dutch: Dierexperimentencommissie / DEC (see DEC constraint above); Instantie voor Dierenwelzijn / IvD - German: Tierversuchskommission / TvK (advisory committee under §15 Tierschutzgesetz) - French: Comité d'éthique en expérimentation animale / CEEA; Comité d'éthique animale - Spanish: Comité de ética en experimentación animal / CEEA

Approval phrasing - Ethics/Ethical (approval|clearance) [was] (granted|obtained|received|given|secured) - Ethically approved - Approved by the (ethics|irb|institutional|independent|local|review|research) ... - This/The study/protocol/experiment/procedures/methods/research [was] (approved|reviewed) by - Study was ethically approved - (Followed|met|follow) the ethical (guidelines|standards|requirements) - In accordance with ... ethical (guidelines|standards) - Ethics protocol - Approved under (protocol|reference|number)

Waiver / exemption - Ethics/Ethical (waiver|exemption) - IRB (waiver|exemption|exempt) - Exempted from (ethics|irb|institutional review) - Waived by the (ethics|irb|institutional|review) (committee|board) - Deemed exempt

Declaration of Helsinki - Declaration of Helsinki / Helsinki Declaration

Patterns are NOT designed to capture: - General ethical considerations or ethical dilemmas in study content - Mentions of “ethics” in theoretical or philosophical contexts - Author approval of a manuscript (e.g. “all authors approved the final version”) - Ethical behaviour as a measured variable (e.g. “ethical decision-making”) - URLs containing “ethics” in path components

Live data collection is detected by the internal helper .detect_live_data(), which searches for sentences indicating that data were collected directly from human or animal participants. Papers without any live-data signal are not flagged as missing ethics approval. The helper uses conservative patterns to avoid flagging secondary data analyses, computational experiments, or economics papers that analyse existing survey data. See .detect_live_data() for the full list of patterns and intentional exclusions.

A paper that states that no human or animal subjects took part (“no human subjects were involved”, “did not involve human participants”, or people taking part “not as subjects”) is not expected to have an ethics statement, whatever participant phrase it also has (see .detect_no_participants()). A negation near a participant phrase alone (“No participants were excluded”) does not count: it reports a study with participants.

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Power Analysis Check works

This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size.

The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information.

The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as ‘a-priori’, ‘sensitivity’, or ‘post-hoc’. Note that ‘post-hoc’ or ‘observed’ power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word ‘power’. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science.

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine, Daniel Lakens and Cristian Mesquida

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value).

How Preregistration Check works

Retrieve information from preregistrations in a standardised way, and make them easier to check.

The Preregistration Check module identifies preregistrations on the OSF and AsPredicted based on links in the manuscript, retrieves the preregistration text, and organizes the information into a template. The module retrieves text from the OSF with its API, and from AsPredicted with ResearchBox’s API when a ResearchBox key is set (see rbox_token()), or else from the preregistration’s web page. The information in the preregistration is returned. An AsPredicted link that could not be read is named in the report, with the reason.

The module can’t extract information from non-structured preregistration templates (i.e., where the preregistration is uploaded in a single text field) and it can’t retrieve information in preregistrations that are stored as text documents on the OSF.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download information from other preregistration sites, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Marginal Significance works

List all sentences that describe an effect as ‘marginally significant’.

The marginal module searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The list of terms is a subset of those listed in a blog post by Matthew Hankins. The module returns all sentences that match terms describing ‘marginally significant’ results.

Some of the terms identified might not be problematic in some contexts, and there are ways to describe ‘marginal significance’ that are not detected by the module.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 51 papers with 87 statements, this module correctly identified 38 statements (true positives) and incorrectly flagged 22 statements (false positives). It failed to detect 27 statements. Thus, among all statements flagged by the module, 63% were genuine cases (positive predictive value). However, the module missed 42% of all true statements (false negative rate).

How StatCheck works

Check consistency of p-values and test statistics

The Statcheck module runs Statcheck. Statcheck searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern, and identifies APA reported statistical tests. More information on the package can be found at https://github.com/cran/statcheck. The module only returns Statcheck results for t-tests and F-tests, as these are the only tests which have been validated, see https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/.

Statcheck was developed by Michèle Nuijten and Sascha Epskamp.

Statcheck considers p = 0.000 an error, as you should report p < 0.001. Furthermore, p < 0.03 is an error if the p-value was 0.031, and one should simply report exact p-values (p = 0.031). Statcheck might miss one-sided tests, and falsely assume the p-value is incorrect. For more information, see StatCheck.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 685 tests with 34 instances of inconsistent reporting, Statcheck correctly detected 34 of them, and incorrectly identified 26. Therefore 0% of true instances were missed, and 43% of detections were false positives. See https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/tcxaj_v1/ for more details of the validation.

How Exact P-Values works

List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000).

This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001.

A p-value that is not the result of a test is not flagged: a table note (“* p < .05, ** p < .01”), a figure legend (“Asterisks indicate significant differences (p < .05)”, “Values in bold are significant at p < .05”) or a stated threshold (“p < .05 was considered significant”, “thresholded at p < .001”). GROBID often puts such notes into the running text, so each p-value is judged by the words in its own clause (the text up to a “;” or a full stop), and never left out when a test statistic belongs to it (“F(1, 7) = 8.03, # p < .05”). The column not_a_test of the table says why a p-value was left out (“marker”, “threshold” or “legend”). Notes in other forms, such as a marker after the p-value (“p < .05 (*)“), are still flagged.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (“decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table’s footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above).

This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value).

How Non-Significant P Value Check works

This module checks for imprecisely reported p values. If p > .05 is detected, it warns for misinterpretations.

The nonsignificant p-value check searches for regular expressions that match a predefined pattern. The module identifies all p-values in a manuscript and selects those that are not reported to be smaller than or equal to 0.05. It returns all sentences containing non-significant p-values.

In the future, the Metacheck team aims to incorporate a machine learning classifier to only return sentences likely to contain misinterpretations. If you want to help to improve the module, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 194 papers with 1602 instances of non-significant p-values, this module correctly detected 1486 of them, and incorrectly identified 153. Additionally, 91% of detections were true instances (positive predictive value). That is, when this module flags non-significant p-values in a paper, it correctly identifies an issue 91% of the time.

How Effect Sizes in t-tests and F-tests works

The Effect Size module checks if effect sizes are correctly reported in t-tests and F-tests.

The Effect Size check searches for regular expressions that match typical ways in which effect sizes are reported. It subsequently checks different ways in which Cohen’s d, g, ηp2, and ωp2 can be computed against the reported value. If effects are missing, or might be incorrect, you the module provides a warning. The module was validated on APA reported statistical tests, and might miss effect sizes that were reported in other reporting styles. It was validated by the Metacheck team on papers published in Psychological Science.

This module only checks statistical results reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process statistics reported only in tables.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: In a sample of 161 papers with 1469 tests, this module correctly detected 1106 reported effect sizes (true positives) and correctly identified 295 cases where no effect size was present (true negatives). However, it missed 23 that were reported (false negatives), and incorrectly identified 45 effect sizes when none were reported (false positives). Among all instances detected by the module, 96% were true cases (positive predictive value). In a validation against 221 reported Cohen’s d effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 218 cases (99%). In a validation against 485 partial eta-squared effect sizes, it correctly indicated coherence in 480 (99%)

How Codebook Check works

This module checks whether the data columns in a repository are documented in a codebook or README. It locates codebook/readme files, extracts the variable definitions they contain, matches those definitions against the data columns extracted by data_check, and reports documentation coverage: how many data columns are documented, and which documented variables are never used.

The Codebook Check module consumes the columns and file classification produced by data_check (and, transitively, repo_check). Files classified as codebook or readme are parsed with parse_codebook(), which reads structured tables (CSV/TSV/Excel with a variable-name column and a label column), embedded labels in haven files (SPSS/Stata/SAS), and plain text from rich-text formats (docx/pdf/rtf/odt). Embedded haven labels from data files are also harvested directly.

Each data column is then matched against the parsed variable definitions with match_column_labels(), using normalised-name matching with experiment-group scoping, haven-label priority, and rule-based label-equivalence merging.

Beyond the variable label, the module harvests the DDI-style per-variable properties a source supplies: the value labels / code list (the 1=“Strongly disagree”…5=“Strongly agree” mapping — from SPSS/Stata value labels and from a codebook “values”/“coding” column), the missing-value scheme (which codes denote missingness, from haven declared missings and labels that read as “refused”/“n/a”), and question text and columns when present. These are carried onto the matched data columns and exported into the Psych-DS variableMeasured (as a schema.org code list plus namespaced metacheck: fields).

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE). When llm_use(TRUE), three optional LLM tiers run: parsing unstructured codebook text that the rules could not handle, fuzzy-matching still-unlabelled columns to still-unmatched codebook variables, and merging conflicting label definitions into a single canonical label.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the codebook_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Repository Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories.

The Repository Check module lists files on the OSF, GitHub, ResearchBox, DSpace (PsychArchives and other legacy- and DSpace 7-based installations), Zenodo, Dataverse, Figshare, Dryad, ReShare, 4TU.ResearchData, Mendeley Data, DataONE (Arctic Data Center, KNB, and other member nodes), and LDbase based on links in the manuscript.

Listing a repository’s files never requires an API key, but some hosts answer faster or more completely with one: OSF allows 100 requests/hour unauthenticated versus 10,000/day with a token (see [osf_pat()]), and Dryad enforces a strict per-IP daily quota on repeated listing (see cache below). Dryad is a special case beyond rate limits: listing a Dryad dataset’s files works without a key, but actually downloading file CONTENTS from Dryad fails with HTTP 401 unless a key is set, even for a fully public dataset (see [dryad_pat()] or [dryad_auth()]). Since this module only lists files and never downloads their contents itself, that limitation applies to data_check and code_check (which do download content), not here – see their own documentation.

When a linked OSF page is a registration, its registered_from project (the one it was registered from, which the manuscript itself may never link directly) is also checked: if that project is public its files are listed under its own URL, and if it is closed or otherwise inaccessible the report flags it explicitly, since some registrations only describe their content rather than mirroring it.

If you want to extend the package to be able to download files from additional data repositories reach out to the Metacheck development team.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the repo_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Code Check works

This module retrieves information from repositories checked by repo_check about code files (R, Python, SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, MATLAB).

The Code Check module checks R (also R Markdown and Quarto), Python (also Jupyter notebooks), SAS, SPSS, Stata, Mplus, and MATLAB files, using regular expressions to check the code; JASP files are listed but not read. The language of a Quarto document or a notebook is read from the file itself (its engine or kernel), not from its extension. The regular expression search will detect the number of comments, the lines at which libraries/imports are loaded, attempts to detect absolute paths to files, setwd() and install.packages() calls, and lists files that are loaded, and checks if these files are in the repository; R code is also parsed. The module will return suggestions to improve the code if there are no comments, if libraries/imports are loaded in lines further than 4 lines apart, if files that are loaded are not in the repository, if absolute file paths, setwd() or install.packages() are found, and if R code cannot be parsed.

The regular expressions can miss information in code files, or falsely detect parts of the code as a fixed file path. Libraries/imports might be loaded in one block, even if there are more than 3 intermittent lines. The module was tried out internally on papers published in Psychological Science, but has not been formally validated. There might be valid reasons why some loaded files can’t be shared, but the module can’t evaluate these reasons, and always gives a warning.

The module also checks whether the repository pins the R/package versions the analysis actually depended on: an renv.lock file (parsed for the R version and every locked package + its version/source), a sessionInfo()/sessioninfo::session_info() text dump (matched by filename — sessionInfo.txt/session_info.txt and similar, or embedded in a README), or a groundhog::groundhog.library()/checkpoint::checkpoint() date-pin call in the code (a bare library(groundhog)/library(checkpoint) does not count — the pinning call itself must be present). When none of these is found, the report flags it as a reproducibility gap: package versions may drift between when the analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt.

If you want to extend the package to perform additional checks on code files, or make the checks work on other types of code files, reach out to the Metacheck development team.

Checking code requires downloading its file contents. For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this never succeeds unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (listing the repository’s files does not need one). Without a key, every Dryad-hosted code file is listed but unchecked, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures recorded in the manifest.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Raphael Merz

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the code_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Data Check works

This module classifies the files in a repository into semantic types (data, codebook, code, software, output, supplemental, readme, asset, other) and, for tabular data files, extracts each column’s type and summary statistics.

The Data Check module consumes the file list produced by repo_check (or any files added via local_path). Each file is classified with rule-based heuristics layered over metacheck’s file_category() and file_types: file names matching README / codebook patterns win first, then an extension crosswalk, then format-locked extension overrides. For every file classified as tabular data that is available locally, the module reads the file head, describes each column with data_col_facets() and computes summary statistics for numeric columns. Every sheet of a spreadsheet that holds a table is read: a file with several such sheets has its columns under source_file = "file.xlsx [sheet]", and the sheet column names the sheet of any spreadsheet with several sheets; a sheet of notes or a codebook is treated as documentation when the file has another table. Following DDI, a column is described by orthogonal facets rather than a single type: representation (numeric/text/datetime/code — how it is stored), measurement_level (Stevens: nominal/ordinal/interval/ratio), concept (what it measures: reaction_time/age/gender/likert/id/…), role (identifier/measure/condition/timestamp), unit, and a quality state (ok/empty/constant). Concepts are detected by name+value rules (the demographic concepts via data_check_demographic()); when llm_use(TRUE) the model fills concepts and measurement levels the rules left blank. Qualtrics survey exports are recognised (data_check_is_qualtrics()): their extra header rows are stripped so columns type correctly, and the reserved response-metadata columns (StartDate, Duration, Finished, …) are tagged.

The module defaults to rules-only when llm_use(FALSE): columns the rules cannot resolve (ambiguous 3–20-unique integers, ambiguous character columns) fall back to continuous / text respectively. When llm_use(TRUE), ambiguous columns and unresolved file types (other) are sent to llm() for optional refinement, and every file is assigned a study group (ex1, pilot2, shared, …) so that multi-study repositories can be recognised (used by psychds_check). Without an LLM the study group is left NA (unknown).

Column extraction requires files to be readable from disk. Files fetched by repo_check from OSF/GitHub/etc. without a local copy (file_location is NA) are classified but not column-extracted; pass local_path to point at a downloaded copy of the repository.

For a paper whose repository is on Dryad, this means column extraction never happens unless a Dryad API key is set: Dryad requires one to download file bytes, even from a fully public dataset (dataset listing and metadata do not need one). Without a key, every Dryad file stays classified but un-downloaded, column_n is 0, and a warning naming Dryad and ?dryad_pat/?dryad_auth is included among the download failures. A one-time session message is also shown (see repo_check) the first time a Dryad dataset is encountered with no key set.

Every downloaded text file the authors wrote (code, settings, survey definitions such as Qualtrics .qsf files, documentation, outputs) is searched for keys: API keys, access tokens and private keys, which let anyone who downloads the file use a paid service at the authors’ cost. Of a tabular data file only the column names and first 3 rows of the table as read are searched: its values come from participants, but a key the authors set for a whole survey (as embedded data in a Qualtrics survey flow) is exported in every response. The search uses the rules of the secret scanner betterleaks (https://github.com/betterleaks/betterleaks, MIT licence) of high and medium confidence. A key found turns the traffic light red; the report and the keys table give its file, line and type, and only its beginning. Other files over 25 MB and binary files are not searched. A key is never tested with its provider. Every module’s result has any whole key replaced by “keyremoved” (see module_run()).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Levi Baruch

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Validation: This module has not been validated. All checks in the data_check module have unknown error rates. Carefully evaluate the output of this module. You can help improve this module by reporting an issue on GitHub.

How Reproducibility Check works

This module assesses whether a paper’s R and Python code can be run on its data. It works in two phases. The static phase (always run) collects the package dependencies the code declares, rewrites the data-file paths that do not work in the repository as the authors organised it, works out the order the scripts must run in, and diagnoses why any referenced input file is unavailable — reporting what a reproduction attempt would involve and where it is likely to break. The execution phase (opt-in, execute = TRUE) then actually runs the code: it copies the repository into a throwaway directory, optionally installs the declared dependencies into a throwaway library, runs each script in order in an isolated subprocess with a per-script timeout, and captures the outcome and full output of each run.

By default (execute = FALSE) the module does not run any code — it performs only static analysis: reading dependencies with the same extractors as code_check, finding the files the code references in the repository, and building a run-order dependency graph. It reports what would be installed and run rather than doing it.

When execute = TRUE, the module additionally runs the downloaded code on your machine — a deliberate, opt-in action gated behind that argument (callr is required for R code). Each script runs in an isolated subprocess so a crash cannot take down the R session; note this isolates crashes, not the filesystem or network. Installs (when install_missing = TRUE) and the throwaway run library never touch your main R library. Each script’s outcome is one of ran_ok, errored, timed_out, dependency_unavailable, not_parsed, run_by_source (an R script another script runs with source(), which is run only inside that script, since on its own it lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first), run_by_import (a Python file other files import, a module rather than a script, unless it has an if __name__ == "__main__": block), jags_model (a JAGS or BUGS model saved with an R extension, which another script reads) or not_r_content (a file that is not R at all, such as a JSON or HTML dump); these last two are not run and are not failures. python2 marks Python 2 code that was not run. With sandbox = "docker" such code runs with Python 2.7 (option metacheck.docker_image_py2; FALSE turns this off), which modifications records; it is never converted, since that can change results. defines_functions is a file that only defines functions, which is used, not run (table$used_by names the scripts that use it), and not_analysis is a file of software rather than of the analysis: a package’s code, tests, documentation or setup.py, a copy of a tool, a web application, a script a program wrote (table$not_analysis_why says which); neither is run or counted as a script. docker_failed means the container never started, which says nothing about the script, so it keeps the light from being green but does not make it red. needs_a_person is a script that stopped because it asks a person to choose a file or answer a question, or that starts an app, and needs_internet one that stopped because the network is off in a Docker run, or, with internet = TRUE, could not reach what it asked for; download_too_large is a script stopped for downloading more than the limits allow (see internet), and out_of_memory one that, or a program it started (such as a compiler), ran out of the memory each script may use. All four are treated the same way. not_downloaded is a script that stopped on a file the repository lists but that was not downloaded, such as one over max_file_size: it could not be tried, so it is not counted as a script that did not reproduce (summary_table$repro_not_downloaded_n counts them apart). not_read is a file metacheck could not read, so it was not run; the light is then not green, as the file may read and run on another computer, and table$error_message says why, naming a package that is installed but cannot be loaded on the computer that ran the check. empty is a file with nothing in it, which is not run or counted as a script. For a script that did not run through, table$error_message is its error, short (at most 300 characters): the error line of its output, which names a package that is not there, with the address it asked for when it needed the internet, or the time limit it reached; table$reason sorts it into a kind. A timeout means “still running at the cutoff”, not a failure, so raise timeout for legitimately long-running (e.g. Bayesian) scripts. dependency_unavailable means the script’s own package could not be installed from live CRAN, the CRAN Archive, or a named GitHub/URL source — an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so unlike errored/timed_out it does not force the traffic light red. The full stdout/stderr of every run is kept in the result’s run_results (the report shows it in per-script dropdowns, capped for readability). The traffic light reflects the STATIC readiness signals by default, but an execution error (errored/timed_out) does recolour it to red — a script that crashes on its own analysis is a genuine reproduction failure. A script that fails with could not find function is run once more with the library() calls the project’s other scripts make added at its top (or the one package that exports the function, or magrittr for %>%), and a script that then runs is reported as reproducible only after that repair.

Dependencies are reported name-only, with the source (CRAN, GitHub, or a base package already shipped with R) — static analysis of the code cannot know which version was used, and running against current package versions is itself informative: a break argues the authors should have pinned versions. When the repository does record versions, a run with recorded_versions = TRUE installs the packages the scripts load at those versions, but it does not change the R version, which remains a limitation of the check.

Run order is derived from read-after-write data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads must run first), source() edges, and numeric filename prefixes as a weak tie-breaker. Ambiguous orderings, dependency cycles, and inputs a script reads but that no earlier script produces (and that are not in the repository) are surfaced as warnings, since these are the situations most likely to make an otherwise-correct reproduction fail.

Python code (.py files, and notebooks and Quarto documents whose code is Python, from which the code is extracted first) goes through the same two phases, reported in its own “Python code” section. Each file is checked for syntax errors with Python’s own parser when a Python interpreter (python, or else python3) is available; dependencies are read from the import statements, with versions from a requirements.txt or pyproject.toml when there is one, and installed with pip; each script runs as its own python process (processx is required), so unlike R scripts, a name one script defines is not available to another. When no Python interpreter is available, the Python files are reported as not run and the R results are still returned. Statistics the Python scripts print are compared with the paper together with the R output and any self-reproducible output (JASP/jamovi, SPSS-Viewer, notebook outputs).

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

The ability to infer others' mental states is central to understanding human behavior.

Across four studies (total N = 827), we examined how facial information and perceivers' conceptual knowledge structure mental-state inferences. In Study 1, participants identified 60 complex mental states more accurately from full faces than from faces with the eye region removed or isolated eye regions, demonstrating the importance of information beyond the eyes.

Study 2 showed that mental states believed to co-occur were perceived as more similar in facial appearance. Crucially, perceivers' idiosyncratic conceptual associations predicted their own facial-similarity judgments even after accounting for associations shared across participants.

Studies 3 and 4 extended this correspondence from perceptual similarity to categorical identification: conceptually associated states were more likely to be confused with one another, both for standardized posed expressions and for naturalistic, unposed faces. On trials involving misidentification, participants' unique conceptual associations predicted which incorrect mentalstate label they selected above and beyond shared conceptual structure. Together, these findings suggest that inferring mental states from faces depends on both distributed facial information and the conceptual organization perceivers bring to the task. More broadly, they identify individual differences in conceptual knowledge as a source of systematic variation in how people read minds from the same facial expressions.

[div-01]

Statement of public significance: People often assume that understanding what someone is thinking or feeling is a matter of reading their facial expressions, especially their eyes, but our findings suggest that these judgments also depend on what observers believe about how different mental states relate to one another. Across four studies, we found that facial information beyond the eyes helps people recognize complex mental states, while states believed to occur together tend to be perceived as more similar in facial appearance and are more likely to be confused with one another. Importantly, individuals' unique beliefs about how mental states relate predicted their own perceptual judgments and specific errors beyond associations shared with others, even when viewing naturalistic faces, suggesting that two people looking at the same expression may interpret it differently partly because they bring different conceptual understandings of other minds to what they see.

Reading Minds Beyond the Eyes: Conceptual Knowledge Structures Mental State Perception

Understanding others' thoughts, emotions, and intentions requires inferring mental states, a process known as mentalizing or mind-reading (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001). Extensive work has explored the cognitive mechanisms underlying mental state inferences using explicit information (Barrett et al., 2011; Byom & Mutlu, 2013; Ho et al., 2022; Hudson et al., 2016; Mitchell, 2009; Saxe & Kanwisher, 2003). Far less clear, however, are the visual cues perceivers use to infer such states during social interactions.

For canonical emotions (e.g., joy, fear), decades of research show that people reliably distinguish emotional categories from facial expressions (Ekman, 1993; Ekman et al., 1987; Jack et al., 2016). Recent work using naturalistic face-body expressions found that perceivers can distinguish 28 unique mental state dimensions (e.g., confusion, doubt, sympathy; Cowen & Keltner, 2020) 1 , yet the visual cues enabling such granular mental-state representations remain unclear.

Much attention has focused on the role of the eyes in conveying mental states (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Lee & Anderson, 2017; Looser & Wheatley, 2010). The well-known Reading the Mind in the Eyes test demonstrates that observers can infer nuanced states such as suspicion or curiosity from the eye region alone, i.e., the eyes and eyebrows (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001).

The eyes convey not only strictly emotional states but also cognitively rich states like awe through cues such as gaze direction or eye-widening (Lee & Anderson, 2017). Yet the role of other facial features in mental-state perception remains unclear. Although perceivers are sensitive to a wide range of facial cues, these have been studied primarily in the context of recognizing canonical emotional expressions (e.g., anger, joy; Dimberg et al., 2000; Ekman & Oster, 1979; Smith et al., 2005), and less is known about how they contribute to perceiving complex mental states (e.g., skepticism, curiosity).

Research shows that people engage in holistic and configural processing of faces, such that individual features are perceived in relation to one another and to the face as a whole (Calder et al., 2000; Tanaka & Farah, 1993; Young et al., 1987). While some studies suggest that mental-1 Throughout our work, we define mental states as internal, latent states, cognitive or affective, that occupy the mind without being overtly expressed. This definition is intentionally broad and context-agnostic, encompassing moods and emotions as well as cognitive processes such as planning and reasoning (Thornton et al., 2023).

state inferences from the eyes alone can be as accurate as those from full faces (Baron-Cohen et al., 1997), those findings rested on a narrow set of states. We propose that perceivers will be more accurate when viewing full faces because they integrate a broader set of cues. Other expressive cues, such as those from the mouth, are important for nonverbal communication and may also contribute broadly to mental-state perception (Jack & Schyns, 2015; Wegrzyn et al., 2017).

Beyond visual cues themselves, contextual factors such as situational cues and prior conceptual knowledge contribute to the recognition of emotions and social categories (Barrett et al., 2011; Freeman & Ambady, 2011; Zaki et al., 2009), and are likely to influence mental state inferences. We propose that top-down conceptual knowledge, specifically, perceivers' understanding of how mental states relate to one another, plays a critical role in shaping mental state judgments. For example, if confusion is conceptually related to skepticism in a perceiver's mind, that perceiver may rely on visually similar facial cues to perceive both states. Such conceptual influences could shape the accuracy of these inferences.

Study 1

In Study 1, we examined whether accuracy in detecting 60 unique mental states from faces is higher for full faces than partial facial cues. Participants viewed images of either full faces, faces without the eye region, or the eye region alone, and selected the expressed mental state from four options. We predicted that participants would be more accurate in judging mental states from full faces compared to cropped faces or eyes/eyebrows alone.

Method

Participants

All participants provided informed consent and received financial compensation. Primary English-speaking U.S. residents were recruited, targeting at least 30 participants per stimulus (Hehman et al., 2018; Stolier et al., 2018) and oversampling to account for exclusions. A total of 150 participants were recruited via Prolific (Mage = 41.31, SDage = 14.50; two implausible age responses excluded; 93 females, 56 males, 1 another gender; 113 White, 17 Black, 5 Asian, 10 Multiracial, 5 another race).

Stimuli

We selected 60 out of 93 mental states from the McGill Face Database (Schmidtmann et al., 2020). In the database, each mental state is portrayed by two actors (one male, one female).

Each actor had been instructed to portray every mental state, and their portrayals were validated by independent raters using a four-alternative forced-choice procedure. The 60 mental states we selected were recognized above chance for both the male and female actor. For each of the 120 images (60 male, 60 female), we generated two cropped versions: one isolating the eye region and one with the eye region removed. Each of the 120 original faces thus appeared in three versions: full-face, face-without-eyes, or eyes-only (see Figure 1). For clarity, "eyes-only" denotes the cropped eyes-and-eyebrows region.

Procedure

Participants were randomly assigned to evaluate a subset of 360 stimuli comprising 20 male and 20 female images in each of the three cropping conditions (full-face, face-without-eyes, eyes-only). To ensure independence of ratings, if a participant saw a given mental state (e.g., "Sarcastic") for a given actor in one condition (e.g., female full-face), that stimulus was not presented again in the remaining conditions. Across the three blocks, participants evaluated all 60 mental states twice each, once for a male face and once for a female face, with condition assignment randomized. On average, each stimulus (actor × mental state × cropping condition) was rated by 50 participants.

On each trial, participants viewed a stimulus alongside four response options, one corresponding to the correct mental state. The three foils were quasi-randomly selected from the remaining 59 mental states, and option order was randomized across participants. Before beginning, participants were informed that they would view images of faces or eyes displaying different mental state expressions and were instructed to identify the depicted mental state ("What is this person's mental state experience?").

Ten attention checks were distributed across the three blocks. Across all studies, participants who failed more than two were excluded. No participants met this criterion in Study 1.

Transparency and Openness

None of the studies were preregistered. All de-identified data, study materials, and analysis code are available on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/brj3t/overview?view_only=6c01249b7816414e9df0859241fe2ea7). Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 was used to assist with refining the R analysis scripts. Note. Example of the face stimuli used in Study 1: full-face mental state stimulus with no cropping, cropped image displaying only the eye region (enlarged, as presented to participants), and cropped image of the face with the eye region removed.

Results

Average accuracy was calculated separately for each participant in the full-face, eyesonly, and face-without-eyes conditions. One-sample t-tests confirmed that accuracy in detecting mental states was significantly above chance (25%) in all three conditions. As expected, accuracy was above chance for the full-face condition (M = 65.27%, SD = 11.12%; t(149) = 44.33, p < .001, d = 3.62) and the eyes-only condition (M = 51.47%, SD = 11.05%; t(149) = 29.33, p < .001, d = 2.40), consistent with prior work (Baron-Cohen et al., 1997). More importantly, participants also showed above-chance accuracy in the face-without-eyes condition (M = 57.33%, SD = 10.70%; t(149) = 37.02, p < .001, d = 3.02), indicating that cues outside the eye region support mental state recognition.

A repeated-measures ANOVA revealed significant differences in accuracy across conditions, F(2.00, 297.43) = 104.88, p < .001, ηp² = .41 (Figure 2). Follow-up pairwise comparisons with Holm correction showed that participants were significantly more accurate in identifying mental states when viewing full faces than when viewing eyes-only, t(149) = 14.19, p < .001, or faces-without-eyes, t(149) = 8.27, p < .001. Perhaps surprisingly, accuracy in the facewithout-eyes condition was also significantly higher than in the eyes-only condition, t(149) = 6.26, p < .001, highlighting the importance of cues beyond the eye region in facilitating mental state inferences. Note. Each data point represents an individual participant's accuracy score. Violin plots depict the distribution of accuracy across the three conditions (full-face, eyes-only, and face-withouteyes). The red dashed line indicates chance-level accuracy (.25) for mental state identification. Black points within the violins represent condition means, with the upper and lower bounds indicating 95% confidence intervals.

Discussion

In Study 1, we found above-chance accuracy in detecting 60 complex mental states from all facial feature conditions. Cropped faces with the eye region removed not only elicited abovechance accuracy but permitted more accurate inferences than the eye region alone. These findings extend previous research by highlighting that facial features beyond the eye region contribute to accurate mental state detection, suggesting that prior work may have underestimated their importance in mental state judgments.

Study 2

Study 1 established that mental-state judgments draw on information distributed across the face. Study 2 turned to how perceivers interpret that information, testing whether their conceptual knowledge of how mental states relate corresponds to the structure they perceive in facial expressions. We predicted that states believed to co-occur would be perceived as perceptually more similar.

Method

Participants

With 60 mental states, there are 1,770 unique pairs (e.g., perplexed and suspicious).

Following prior work with similar designs (Bin Meshar et al., 2022; Hehman et al., 2018; Stolier et al., 2018), we aimed to collect ratings from ~30 participants per pair. To minimize fatigue, each participant was randomly assigned to judge a subset of 118 pairs across 15 counterbalanced subsets, yielding a target sample of 450 participants. A total of 451 participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk. Participants who failed more than two attention checks were excluded (n = 93). The final sample included 358 participants (Mage = 38.30 years, SDage = 10.31 years; 149 female, 207 male, 1 other, 1 declined to answer; 286 White, 43 Black, 14 Asian, 15 another race). All primary analyses were replicated with the full sample (N = 451) to ensure robustness, and these exclusions had a negligible impact on the pattern of results.

Stimuli

We used the original full-face versions of the 120 stimuli from Study 1 (60 mental states conveyed by two actors).

Procedure

Each participant completed a face similarity judgment task followed by a conceptual association task. On each trial, participants evaluated the similarity between two mental state expressions. There were 1,770 unique pairwise associations among the 60 mental states. Each participant was assigned to judge 118 pairs both perceptually and conceptually.

Face Similarity Judgments. Participants viewed two photos of the same actor conveying the two mental states in a given pair, displayed side by side (e.g., for the pair perplexed and suspicious, participants saw the same actor expressing each state). Half of the 118 pairs featured the female actor and the other half the male actor, counterbalanced across participants.

Participants rated the similarity of the two facial expressions on a 7-point scale (1 = Not at all similar,7 = Extremely similar). Presentation order was randomized, and three attention checks were included.

Conceptual Association Task.

Participants then rated their conceptual associations for the same mental state pairs. For each pair, participants answered the question "At any given moment, how likely is a person to be [perplexed] and [suspicious]?" on a 7-point scale (1 = Not at all likely,7 = Extremely likely). Four attention checks were included.

Results

We first tested whether shared conceptual structure corresponded to shared perceptual structure, and then asked the stronger person-specific question of whether individuals' unique conceptual associations predicted corresponding differences in their own perceptions.

Group-Level Association

We first examined the correspondence between conceptual associations and perceptual similarity at the group level. For each measure, we constructed a 60 × 60 similarity matrix averaged across participants: one capturing face similarity judgments and one capturing conceptual associations. Each cell in the face similarity matrix denotes the average similarity rating of each state pair, while each cell in the conceptual association matrix denotes the average conceptual association between state pairs. We then assessed the correspondence between the two matrices using representational similarity analysis (RSA; Kriegeskorte, 2008), computing a Spearman rank correlation across the 1,770 unique off-diagonal values. Spearman's rank correlation was used to not assume a linear relationship between the two measures (Kriegeskorte, 2008).

As shown in Figure 3, the results revealed a strong positive correlation between the conceptual association matrix and the face similarity matrix, Spearman's 𝜌(1768) = .513, p < .001; 95% CI = [0.476, 0.549]. Thus, as predicted, the more strongly associated participants judged two mental states to be (e.g., perplexed and suspicious), the more similar they perceived the corresponding facial expressions to be.

Individual-Level Associations

To distinguish shared conceptual structure from perceivers' idiosyncratic associations, we decomposed each participant's conceptual rating for each mental-state pair into two components: the mean rating for that pair among all other participants (i.e., a leave-one-participant-out group mean) and the participant's deviation from that mean. We entered both components simultaneously into a linear mixed-effects model predicting face similarity judgments, with random intercepts for participants and mental-state pairs. Shared conceptual associations strongly predicted perceived facial similarity, b = .716, SE = .029, t = 24.84, p < .001, 95% CI [.660, .773]. Critically, participants' idiosyncratic departures from this shared conceptual structure also predicted their own face similarity judgments, b = .134, SE = .005, t = 27.89, p < .001, 95% CI [.124, .143]. Thus, when an individual viewed two mental states as more strongly associated than other people did, that individual also perceived the corresponding facial expressions as more similar. Note. (A) Face similarity and conceptual association matrices for all 1,770 pairs of the 60 mental states. Each cell represents one pair. Color reflects where that pair's average rating falls relative to all other pairs in the same matrix, with darker cells indicating greater face similarity or stronger conceptual association. States are ordered by hierarchical clustering of the conceptual association matrix, and the same order is used for both matrices. (B) The subset of states outlined in red in Panel A, enlarged as an example. (C) Face similarity as a function of conceptual

Discussion

Conceptual associations corresponded to mental-state perception at both shared and person-specific levels. States believed to co-occur were perceived as perceptually more similar overall, but critically, participants' idiosyncratic departures from shared conceptual structure predicted corresponding differences in their own perceptual judgments. Thus, individual differences in conceptual organization were reflected in individual differences in how the same mental states were perceived.

Study 3

Study 3 tested whether this conceptual-perceptual correspondence extends beyond similarity judgments to the specific errors people make when identifying mental states. We predicted that stronger conceptual associations would increase the likelihood of confusing one state for another, including at the person-specific level.

Method

Participants

We recruited 221 participants from Prolific. Consistent with previous studies, we aimed for approximately 30 ratings per face stimulus, with oversampling to allow for data cleaning. The 60 mental states were divided into four subsets, each rated by approximately 50 participants.

Participants who failed more than two attention checks and practice trials combined were excluded (n = 4), resulting in a final sample of 217 participants (Mage = 40.48, SDage = 14.46; 138 females, 73 males, 4 identifying as other, and 2 who declined to answer; 161 White, 31 Black, 10 Asian, 15 other).

Stimuli

We used the same 60 mental states from Studies 1 and 2, each depicted by two actors' faces (one male, one female). To reduce participant fatigue, stimuli were divided into four subsets of 15 mental states each. Subsets were created to maximize variability in pairwise conceptual associations. In other words, each subset contained mental state pairs that varied across the full range of conceptual relatedness, from strongly to weakly associated. We achieved this by selecting the four subsets that maximized the standard deviation of mean conceptual association values within each subset, using Study 2 data.

Procedure

Participants began with practice trials designed to familiarize them with the 15 mental states they would judge in the face judgments task. In each practice trial, participants saw a mental state word from their assigned subset (e.g., confused) and selected the matching word from a list of the 15 mental states they would later judge. This word-matching task was intended to reinforce familiarity with the assigned stimulus set. Participants completed 10 practice trials, each randomly drawing from the 15 mental states in their assigned subset.

Face Judgments Task. The face judgments task consisted of two blocks, one for each target actor. In each block, 15 face stimuli, one depicting each assigned mental state, were presented one at a time in randomized order. Thus, participants completed 30 face-judgment trials. On each trial, participants selected the mental state that best matched the target's mental state experience from a list of their 15 assigned mental states. Block order was counterbalanced across participants. Two attention checks were included.

Conceptual Association Task.

Following the face judgments task, participants completed a conceptual association task similar to the one used in Study 2. In this task, they rated the conceptual association between all possible pairs of their 15 assigned mental states, resulting in a total of 105 unique trials. On each trial, participants answered, "At any given moment, how likely is a person to be [perplexed] & [suspicious]?" on a 7-point scale (1 = Not at all likely,7 = Extremely likely). Trial order and the left-right ordering of the two states within each trial were randomized. Six attention checks were included. 2

Results

We first tested whether shared conceptual associations predicted which mental states were confused overall. We then asked whether participants' own conceptual associations predicted their specific errors, including whether idiosyncratic associations explained personspecific confusions beyond the group-level structure.

Face Judgment Confusions

2 Due to a coding error, one mental-state association was missing from a single subset; that association and its corresponding directional face judgment confusions were excluded from all analyses.

For each face stimulus, we calculated the proportion of participants who selected each mental state as their response. For example, for a face depicting amusement, 64% of participants correctly identified it as amused, while relaxed, grateful, flirtatious, and sarcastic were selected 11%, 11%, 10%, and 3% of the time, respectively; all remaining states were selected 1% or less.

Proportions summed to 100% for each face. We then averaged these proportions across the two target actors for each mental state expression.

Each non-correct selection reflected a confusion-a mistaken identification of one mental state as another. For each of the 15 mental states, we therefore calculated 14 confusion scores representing the degree of confusion with every other state. We retained the directionality of these confusions: for instance, an amused face was misidentified as grateful 11% of the time, while a grateful face was misidentified as amused 50% of the time. These were treated as distinct values, resulting in 210 confusion scores per subset (15 mental states × 14 confusion scores).

For conceptual associations, we calculated the average association ratings for each pair of mental states across participants. Since each conceptual association (e.g., amused and grateful) was assessed in only one direction, we assigned the same value to both directional pairs.

For example, if the association between grateful and amused was rated 5 (on the 7-point scale), this value was used for both grateful-amused and amused-grateful pairs. Indeed, a stronger conceptual association between a given pair of mental states was associated with a higher likelihood of confusion between the two states, Spearman's 𝜌(836) = .648, p < .001, 95% CI = [0.605, 0.686] (Figure 4). Thus, at the group level, mental state pairs believed to be more likely to co-occur were also more likely to be confused in perceptual judgments (e.g., mistaking a grateful face for an amused one, or vice-versa).

Individual-Level Associations

We next tested whether perceivers' idiosyncratic conceptual associations predicted the specific errors they made beyond shared conceptual structure. As in Study 2, each participant's conceptual rating for a given state pair was decomposed into the leave-one-participant-out group mean for that pair and the participant's deviation from that mean. Because each face judgment involved a mutually exclusive choice among response labels, we restricted this analysis to trials on which a participant made an error and fit a conditional logistic regression predicting which incorrect label was selected from these shared and idiosyncratic conceptual components, conditioning on each face-judgment trial and clustering standard errors by participant. Shared conceptual associations strongly predicted which incorrect state was selected, b = .968, SE = .030, z = 31.84, p < .001, OR = 2.632, 95% CI [2.480, 2.794]. Critically, participants' idiosyncratic conceptual associations also predicted their specific confusions, b = .061, SE = .016, z = 3.73, p < .001, OR = 1.063, 95% CI [1.029, 1.097], see figure 4. Thus, given that a participant misidentified a face, they were more likely to select a particular incorrect state when they personally viewed that state as more strongly associated with the depicted state than other participants did.

Discussion

Conceptual associations predicted specific mental-state confusions at both shared and person-specific levels. Mental state pairs believed to be more likely to co-occur were more frequently confused in face judgments, and participants were more likely to select a particular incorrect state when they viewed it as more strongly associated with the depicted state, even after accounting for shared associations.

Study 4

Study 3 showed that conceptual structure predicts not only perceived similarity but the specific mental states perceivers confuse, including errors explained by perceivers' idiosyncratic conceptual associations. Study 4 asked whether this correspondence generalizes to naturalistic faces, where facial appearance and expression vary substantially across individuals rather than being constrained by two actors' standardized poses.

Method

Participants

As in Study 3, we aimed to recruit at least 30 participants per stimulus and oversampled to account for data cleaning. Because the study included two versions with different stimuli, we recruited a total of 102 participants through Prolific. No participants met our exclusion criteria of failing more than two practice trials and/or attention checks (Mage = 43.07, SDage = 12.92; 62 females, 40 males; 73 White, 18 Black, 7 Asian, 4 other).

Stimuli

We sought a larger, more naturalistic set of face stimuli than those used in Studies 1-3.

We selected stimuli from Cowen and Keltner (2020), a dataset of 1,500 ambient, naturally occurring faces crowdsourced from millions of individuals worldwide (rather than explicitly posed by actors), each rated by independent raters on 28 emotional states.

We selected faces for which raters agreed that one emotional state was present at 50% intensity or higher, treating that state as the face's perceived primary state. Out of the 28 states in the original dataset, 15 had at least 10 face stimuli meeting this threshold. A complete list of selected stimuli is available on OSF.

For each of the 15 states, we selected the 10 faces with the highest intensity ratings.

When multiple stimuli shared similar intensity values, we prioritized those with the highest image resolution, then selected randomly among remaining ties. This yielded 150 stimuli in total (15 states × 10 faces each). Because this set was too large for a single session, we randomly divided the stimuli into two subsets of 75 faces (five per state), and participants were assigned to one version. This heterogeneity allowed us to test whether conceptual associations predict confusion patterns despite substantial variation in facial appearance and expression. As in Study 3, participants categorized each face using 15 possible mental state response options.

Procedure

The procedure was identical to Study 3, with the only difference being the stimuli evaluated.

Results

As in Study 3, we tested whether conceptual associations predicted perceptual confusions at both shared and person-specific levels, including whether individuals' unique associations predicted their own errors beyond the group-level structure.

Using the same analytic approach as Study 3, we replicated the strong positive association between conceptual associations and patterns of perceptual confusion at the group level, this time with unposed naturalistic faces, Spearman's 𝜌(208) = .572, p < .001, 95% CI = [0.476, 0.656] (Figure 4). When two states were more conceptually related, participants were more likely to confuse those states when judging naturalistic facial expressions. For example, if amusement is believed to co-occur with surprise, then perceivers were more likely to confuse these two states in naturalistic, self-evoked facial expressions.

At the individual level, we again decomposed conceptual associations into the leave-oneparticipant-out group mean for each state pair and each participant's idiosyncratic deviation from that mean. We then used the same conditional-choice analysis as in Study 3, restricting the analysis to erroneous face judgments and predicting which incorrect state was selected while conditioning on each face-judgment trial and clustering standard errors by participant. Shared conceptual associations strongly predicted which incorrect state participants selected, b = .732, SE = .039, z = 18.78, p < .001, OR = 2.080, 95% CI [1.927, 2.245]. Importantly, participants' idiosyncratic conceptual associations also predicted their specific errors, b = .054, SE = .025, z = 2.19, p = .028, OR = 1.056, 95% CI [1.006, 1.109], see Figure 4. Thus, even for naturalistic, unposed faces, participants were more likely to make a particular confusion when they personally viewed the depicted and selected states as more strongly associated than other participants did.

Discussion

Study 4 replicated the correspondence between conceptual structure and mental-state confusions across naturalistic faces, including at the person-specific level after accounting for shared associations. Thus, the relationship generalized beyond standardized posed expressions despite substantial variation in facial appearance and expression. Note. (A, B) Face confusion and conceptual association matrices. Panel A shows one of the four Study 3 stimulus sets as an example (see supplementary materials for all four); Panel B shows the 15 mental states of Study 4. In the confusion matrices, rows are the face shown and columns The predicted probability that an incorrect label is chosen on an error trial. The solid line shows how this probability changes with a pair's shared conceptual association, relative to the average pair; the dashed line shows how it changes when a participant's own rating is higher or lower than the group's. Bands are 95% confidence intervals, points are observed proportions for the shared association, and the gray dotted line indicates chance (1 in 14 incorrect labels).

General Discussion

Across four studies, mental state judgments reflected information distributed across the face as well as perceivers' conceptual associations among mental states. In Study 1, participants were more accurate in identifying mental states from full faces than from partial faces or isolated eye regions. While prior work has emphasized the eyes as the primary window into others' mental states (e.g., Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Lee & Anderson, 2017; Looser & Wheatley, 2010), our findings show that inferences of complex mental states consistently rely on more than the eye region alone. In fact, excluding the eyes permitted more accurate judgments than presenting them in isolation, suggesting that regions like the mouth carry substantial expressive information for complex mental state attributions.

Few studies have challenged the notion that the eyes play a privileged role in communicating mental states. Prior research has found that the most diagnostic facial region varies by mental state: while some states rely more heavily on the eyes, others draw on the mouth or on coordinated movements across regions (Back et al., 2009; Blais et al., 2012; Yuki et al., 2007; Jack et al., 2012). However, this prior research examined basic emotion expressions or a small number of mental states, leaving open whether the importance of non-eye cues extends to the broader range of complex, nuanced states people infer in daily life. The present research demonstrates that across 60 distinct mental states, perceivers rely heavily on cues beyond the eyes, often more so than on the eyes themselves, suggesting that mental state communication depends on a richer constellation of facial information than previously recognized.

In Study 2, we showed that beyond bottom-up facial cues, top-down conceptual associations were also systematically related to mental state perception at both shared and person-specific levels. Mental states that were more strongly associated in the mind were perceived as more visually similar, but importantly, participants' idiosyncratic departures from the group's conceptual structure also predicted their own perceptual judgments. Studies 3 and 4 extended this relationship to specific mental state confusions: participants were more likely to misidentify a depicted state as another state when the two were more strongly conceptually associated. This pattern emerged across both posed and naturalistic expressions, suggesting a robust correspondence between conceptual structure and mental state inference. A growing body of research has shown that conceptual knowledge plays a central role in social categorization, trait attribution, and emotion recognition (e.g., Bin Meshar et al., 2022; Brooks et al., 2019; Freeman et al., 2020; Stolier et al., 2018). Our findings extend this work by demonstrating that both shared and idiosyncratic conceptual structures correspond to how perceivers represent mental states in faces and which states they confuse with one another. While conceptual associations may help scaffold interpretations of complex facial expressions, they may also direct inferences toward related but incorrect mental states. This pattern suggests that more differentiated conceptual representations (i.e., deeming two states as less likely to co-occur) may reduce confusion between them in faces. This is consistent with research on emotional granularity, which links finer-grained emotion representations to more accurate recognition of others' emotional experiences (Israelashvili et al., 2019), greater empathic accuracy, and more effective social support (Erbas et al., 2016; Gregory et al., 2020). This work is not without limitations. Our findings are correlational and do not establish that conceptual knowledge causally alters perception. Conceptual associations may themselves reflect experienced patterns and transitions between mental states (Thornton et al., 2023), creating bidirectional influence. Although the person-specific effects make a purely shared stimulus explanation less likely, they do not resolve causal direction. Future work should manipulate conceptual knowledge directly to test its causal impact on mental-state inference.

In sum, mental-state inference draws on information distributed across the face and the conceptual structure through which perceivers interpret it. Beyond showing that the eyes are not uniquely privileged, our findings reveal that shared and person-specific conceptual associations correspond to which states look alike and which are confused. Conceptual knowledge may therefore explain not only commonalities in how people perceive others' minds, but systematic differences between perceivers confronted with the same social information. Understanding others is not merely a matter of reading faces, but of reading them through a structured model of how mental states relate.

Constraints on Generality

We expect these findings to generalize mostly to mental state judgments from static facial images. Whether these findings extend to dynamic facial expressions remains unknown. In addition, our primary stimuli featured two White young-adult actors posing 60 mental states, which afforded precision and control but limited generalizability. Study 4 partially addressed this by using a more diverse, naturalistic stimulus set. However, systematic comparisons across race, age, and other sociodemographic variables will be important, given that these attributes likely affect mental-state perception through stereotype-based conceptual associations (Freeman & Lin, 2025).

is a Professor of Psychology at Columbia University. This work was supported in part by National Science Foundation Grant BCS-2235130, awarded to

Across four studies, we test a more comprehensive account of how facial cues and conceptual knowledge shape mental-state perception. Study 1 examines whether full facial cues, compared to the eye region alone or all features excluding the eyes, lead to higher inference accuracy across 60 unique mental states. Study 2 tests whether shared and person-specific conceptual associations predict corresponding similarities in perceived facial expressions. Study 3 then examines whether conceptual associations predict specific perceptual confusions between mental states. Finally, Study 4 tests whether these confusion patterns generalize to naturalistic, unposed expressions.
